result.summary: Pausanias describes the sanctuary of Despoena near Acacesium in Arcadia: its portico, the monumental statue group by Damophon, local rites and sacrifices, and nearby shrines including the temple of Pan. He adds digressions on the Titans, Aeschylus, and Despoena's parentage.

scenes.title: Approach and portico of Despoena
scenes.summary: Pausanias walks from Acacesium to the sanctuary, noting the temple of Artemis the Leader, the portico's reliefs, the painted tablet of the mysteries, the portrait of Polybius and the altars.

scenes.title: Damophon's statues and Anytus
scenes.summary: He describes the single-block statues of Despoena and Demeter by Damophon, with Artemis and Anytus beside the throne, and digresses on the Titans, Onomacritus and Aeschylus.

scenes.title: Mirror, Hall and sacred grove
scenes.summary: He describes the mirror, the Hall where mystic rites and sacrifices occur, Despoena's parentage and names, the grove and altars.

scenes.title: Temple of Pan and other shrines
scenes.summary: He climbs to the temple of Pan, recounts its former oracle through Erato, and lists nearby altars and statues.

alias_notes.explanation: Despœna means 'Mistress'; Persephone is her private name, which Pausanias avoids writing.

notable_quotes.reason: Inscription praising Polybius as Greece's missed savior.

analysis.text: Pausanias blends description with religious reticence, withholding mystery cult details from the uninitiated.
The Arcadian cult differs from Panhellenic myth, making Despoena daughter of Poseidon and honouring Polybius, showing local pride in the Achaean statesman.

fun_facts.text: Fragments of Damophon's statue group survive and are displayed in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

language_notes.text: A stade was a Greek unit of about 600 feet (roughly 180 metres), so the temple is less than a kilometre away.
Hercules robbing Apollo of his tripod refers to the myth of Hercules seizing the Delphic tripod; Pausanias promises to tell it at Delphi.
"Dove-tailed in" means joined by interlocking cuts; Pausanias stresses that no piece was added to the sculpture.
A cist is a sacred basket or chest used in mystery rites, holding secret sacred objects.
Refers to Iliad 14, where Hera swears by the gods below in Tartarus, called Titans, to deceive Zeus.
Æschylus made Artemis a daughter of Demeter, following an Egyptian identification with Bubastis; Greeks usually called her daughter of Leto.
Curetes and Corybantes were ecstatic attendants of the Great Mother and the infant Zeus; Pausanias declines to explain, out of religious reticence.
"Hall" translates the Greek megaron, a sacred building for the mysteries, distinct from the temple proper.
Pausanias withholds Despœna's secret name because it belonged to the mystery cult. Pamphus was an early Athenian poet who wrote hymns.
Olive and oak growing from one root: a natural marvel, seen as beyond what a gardener could contrive.
Hippius means "of horses"; Poseidon was worshipped in Arcadia as a horse-god.
Arcas, son of Callisto, was the legendary ancestor of the Arcadians, so Erato's marriage ties Pan's oracle to the nation's origins.

context_notes.text: Polybius, son of Lycortas, was the Arcadian statesman and historian from Megalopolis, who led the Achaean League in the second century BC.
Damophon of Messene was a celebrated sculptor of the second century BC, known for cult statues in the Peloponnese.
Onomacritus was a sixth-century BC Athenian compiler of oracles and Orphic poetry, in which Titans tear apart the infant Dionysus.
Dismembering rather than throat-cutting marks this as an unusual local rite, differing from the standard Greek sacrificial practice.
In Arcadian legend, Poseidon pursued Demeter, who took the form of a mare; Despœna ("the Mistress") was their daughter.
A perpetual fire was a mark of special honor in a sanctuary and required constant tending.
Ares and Aphrodite are named together here; the wooden statue is older, as early Greek cult images were often carved from wood.

literary_notes.text: The inscription's flattering claim, that Greece's ruin came from ignoring Polybius, carries a bitter note, since the statue honours a man whose advice failed to save it.
Pausanias speaks as a discreet initiate, declaring he knows more but withholds it, which adds religious authority and mystery.
The mirror shows the goddesses' statues clearly but the viewer poorly, suggesting the divine is more real than the human onlooker.
Pausanias speaks as a cautious, pious first-person witness, openly respecting religious secrecy and citing earlier authorities.
